seo.title: Karmic tail 6 8 11 compatibility: The Lovers, Justice and Strength
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 8 11 compatibility in the couple's destiny matrix: why love turns into a race here, and what Strength asks of the two people in it.

title: Karmic tail 6-8-11 in compatibility: when love becomes a race
short: The three numbers 6-8-11 in a couple's matrix — The Lovers, Justice and Strength — make one of the most common karmic tails in compatibility: roughly one couple in 23 has it. It is also one of the strangest: no single person can have this tail, only two people together can write it. It is the story of a couple who enter their task through falling in love, walk it like a fair contest with rules, and learn the main thing — a strength that has no need to beat the other.

sections.h2: Why 6-8-11 never appears in a personal destiny matrix
paragraphs: In a personal matrix, the middle of the tail is always the sum of the two outer numbers. A person with The Lovers at the entry and Strength in the task gets 6 + 11 = 17 in the middle — The Star: that personal tail exists, it is 6-17-11. One person never has the triple 6-8-11 anywhere — not in the tail, not in the money, relationship or talent lines: they are built the same way, with the middle equal to the sum of the ends. Anyone searching for "6 8 11 in the destiny matrix" will find these numbers in a row only in a couple's matrix.

In a couple, the middle is added up not from the ends but from the two partners' personal middles. So where one person would have The Star burning, the two of them have Justice. Waite remarks in passing that the figure of Justice "is said to be Astræa". Astraea's name means "the starry one". In the first book of Ovid's Metamorphoses she is the last of the gods to leave the earth — "last of all the virgin deity, Astraea vanished from the blood-stained earth" — and the constellation Virgo, next door to Libra, the Scales, is hers. Our reading: where a single person holds the star of hope, a couple holds a star that has taken up the scales. Not "it'll all work out", but "let's keep it fair".

The second clue is who Strength belongs to. The site's engine went through every date: in no couple with the tail 6-8-11 does either partner have Strength in their personal tail. The couple's Strength is always made of two other cards:

ul: The Hierophant and The Lovers (5 + 6) — in 45.1% of these couples;
The Emperor and The Chariot (4 + 7) — in 29.4%;
Justice and The World (8 + 21 = 29 → 11) — in 11.3%;
The Wheel of Fortune and The Sun (10 + 19 = 29 → 11) — in 9.1%; the other combinations are rarer.

paragraphs: And in 39.6% of couples, neither partner has any of the three cards in their personal tail. Neither of them brings this tail. It appears when the two are added together — like the lions in the myth below: neither hero was a lion, they became lions as a pair.

sections.h2: The myth this couple lives in: Atalanta and Hippomenes
paragraphs: Book Ten of Ovid's Metamorphoses is sung by Orpheus, and inside his song Venus, lying with Adonis on the grass under a poplar, tells him a story, "mingling kisses with her words". The tale is meant to explain why the goddess of love hates lions. Quotations below follow Brookes More's 1922 translation; where a literal rendering matters, it is marked.

Atalanta ran faster than men, and "you could not have said whether her swift speed or her beauty was more worthy of your praise". An oracle told her: "You, Atalanta, never will have need of husband… and while yet living you will lose yourself." She went to live in the woods and set her suitors a condition: "I will not be won… till I am conquered first in speed… A wife and couch shall both be given to reward the swift, but death must recompense the one who lags behind. This must be the condition of a race."

Hippomenes came to watch the race and to condemn the madmen who risked their lives for a wife. He saw her — and begged forgiveness of the men he had just been judging. He challenged her himself. For the first time, Atalanta was unsure whether she wanted to win. Hippomenes prayed to Venus, and she brought him three golden apples from her field on Cyprus. As they ran he threw them one after another, Atalanta turned aside for the gold — and lost.

Having won, Hippomenes forgot to thank Venus. The goddess turned against them both. By a shrine of Cybele, Mother of the gods, she made Hippomenes feel "an untimely desire" (literal translation), the two defiled the sanctuary, and Cybele turned them into lions and took them into her harness. "My dear Adonis keep away from all such savage animals," Venus concludes. Adonis did not listen and was killed hunting. But that is another story.
The three acts of the myth — the meeting, the race, the transformation — come in the same order as the cards of the tail: The Lovers, Justice, Strength.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Lovers: the judge who saw the prize
paragraphs: Hippomenes enters the myth not as a lover but as a judge. He sits watching "the unequal race" (literal translation), "with condemnation in his heart against the racing young men for their headstrong love". Then he sees Atalanta — and passes sentence on himself: "Oh pardon me brave men whom I was blaming, I could not then realize the value of the prize you strove for." As he praises her, his own heart catches fire. The first word of The Lovers in Waite's divinatory list is "Attraction". Attraction overturns a verdict reached before the meeting.

Atalanta's side is subtler. Her gaze grows "softer, in her vacillating hopes to conquer and be conquered" — and further on Ovid says: "she loves and does not know she is in love". Benebell Wen calls The Lovers "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation". Atalanta has only one temptation: to lose.

This is the entry to the task for a 6-8-11 couple. Two such people often recognise each other in an argument, a competition, at work, where one did not give way to the other: what attracts is someone who is not weaker. The couple's common language is teasing, excitement, "who beats whom", and for a long time it stays fun. The couple's wish is to be together as equals. The resistance lives in that same wish: each wants to be the one chosen, and not to lose while at it.

Two more strokes of the myth fall on the difficulties of the entry. Hippomenes, barely in love, is already "full of envy" and "fears for the result": he is afraid someone else will outrun Atalanta — jealousy born of insecurity before there is anything to be jealous about. And Atalanta's oracle names the fear with which people enter this couple: "while yet living you will lose yourself". The condition of the race is her defence against dissolving in another person. The first agreements of such couples often resemble her condition: "only as equals", "nobody owes anybody anything". That is defence, not love, and the task of the entry is to learn to love oneself inside the couple, not only behind a fence of rules.
The roles of the myth are not divided by sex. Either partner can be the runner who sets the conditions, and either can be the judge who traded a verdict for admiration. Quite often they swap places.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Justice: the race Ovid called unequal
paragraphs: The first clue is hidden in a name. Atalanta in Greek comes from ἀτάλαντος, "equal in weight". The root is τάλαντον: scales, the pan of a balance, a measure of weight. The heroine of the myth is named after the scales. She does not need a bridegroom; she needs an equal.

The Justice of the middle shows in the very design of the race. It is a law, and Ovid speaks of it in the language of law: "the condition of a race", and the losers pay "the death-penalty… according to the stipulated bond". In the Latin they "pendunt poenas ex foedere" — they pay up under the compact, and the verb pendere means both "to pay" and "to weigh". The race itself is called unequal: the Latin iniquus means both "unequal" and "unjust" at once, the negation of aequus, "level, fair".

Wen stresses that Justice is "human-made justice", "not the laws of nature or the laws of the divine". Atalanta invented the condition of the race herself: the oracle told her to flee marriage, and she turned the flight into a contract. A 6-8-11 couple also has its own home-made rules: splitting the bill, a rota, who does the dishes, "I had the kids on Saturday — Sunday's yours." In Lisovskaya, Justice in the plus means a fair division of duties, restraint in words, a plan B for everything. As long as the scorekeeping helps both, it holds the couple together.

The second clue is weight. Venus describes the decisive moment of the race like this: "I forced her to turn for it; take it up; and, adding weight to the gold fruit, she held, impeded her with weight and loss of time." A race meant to be fair was decided by weights dropped onto the scales from outside. Golden apples are easy to spot in a couple's life: a present instead of an answer, a lovely surprise that cuts the conversation short and wins the argument, a concession made in order to be produced later. The Justice of the middle asks what the equality rests on: on an agreement — or on who threw the gold more deftly.

Ovid also shows the other side of the same race: "Oh, how often, when she could have passed him, she delayed her speed; and after gazing long upon his face reluctantly again would pass him!" Atalanta gives way out of love — and the race goes on, and the concession counts for nobody. In a couple such slowing down easily becomes a debt in the other's minutes: "I gave that up for you, remember."

The third clue is an unpaid bill. "Adonis, did I not deserve his thanks with tribute of sweet incense? But he was ungrateful, and, forgetful of my help, he gave me neither frankincense nor thanks." Among the tasks of Justice, Lisovskaya lists broken promises, debts and overdue payments, refusing to admit one's own fault. Hippomenes breaks exactly this: help received, payment not made. And Venus turns "against them both" — in the Latin, in ambos. One forgot, and both pay: a couple has one account between two. The scene is familiar: the flat is bought, the wedding is over, the project is delivered — and nobody has said thank you, not to each other, not to those who helped, not to luck. Gratitude is the payment without which the scales later tip into resentment.

And one more line worth remembering. In the thick of her doubts Atalanta exclaims: "But it is not a fault of mine." And Cybele, deciding the fate of the two, finds even the waters of the Styx too mild: "such a punishment seemed light". Among the reversed meanings of Justice, Waite names "excessive severity". This is what the minus of the middle looks like: each keeps their own minutes, the fault is always the other's, and the sentence comes out heavier than the offence.

sections.h2: Main task — Strength: two lions in Cybele's harness
paragraphs: Ovid needs only seven lines for the transformation, and almost each of them is a scene from the life of a couple that has not coped with its main task:

"At once tawny manes cover their smooth necks, their fingers curve into claws, their arms become forelegs, all their weight passes into their chests, and with their tails they sweep the sand. Their faces hold anger; instead of words they give out growls; instead of bridal chambers they haunt the woods; and, feared by others, they champ with tamed teeth the reins of Cybele — lions" (literal translation).

ul: **"Their faces hold anger".** Irritation that does not leave the face even on a quiet evening. The first task of Strength in Lisovskaya is to work with aggression.

**"Instead of words they give out growls".** A quarrel in which both talk and nobody hears — Lisovskaya calls it misunderstanding, "as if speaking different languages". Growling can be silent too: a sigh, a cupboard door banged shut, an answer through gritted teeth.
**"Instead of bridal chambers they haunt the woods".** Closeness gives way to territory: each has their own truth and their own corner.
**"Feared by others".** From outside this is a strong couple with a voice and status, respected and a little feared.

**"They champ with tamed teeth the reins".** The beasts are tamed, but from outside. The two pull one chariot — a mortgage, a business, the children's timetable — honestly, shoulder to shoulder, without ever looking at each other.

paragraphs: The weight Venus added to the apple has not gone anywhere: "all their weight passes into their chests". This is our reading, but Ovid uses the same word both times — pondus, weight — first on the apple, then in the lions' chests.

The darkest version comes from the Roman mythographer Hyginus (Fabulae, 185). In his telling it is Jupiter who punishes, and lions are chosen because they are animals "quibus dii concubitum Veneris denegant" — to whom the gods deny the union of love. The punishment is exact: to stay together for ever and stop being lovers. Lisovskaya has a phrase for this in the minus of Justice: "living like neighbours".

Wen separates two kinds of strength: The Chariot is "the strength to master the world", while Strength is "strength to master the self". Ovid hands the lions to Cybele's reins, and Cybele has long been shown in a chariot drawn by lions: the strength to master oneself becomes the strength to haul a load. That is the danger of this tail: spending one's strength on pulling life along — work, house, status — and leaving none of it for holding oneself. In 29.4% of these couples, the couple's Strength is made of exactly The Emperor and The Chariot of the two partners — two cards of power over the outer world.

Venus's last words sound like a statement of the main task. She tells Adonis to avoid beasts "which do not turn their fearful backs in flight but offer their bold breasts to your attack", so that his courage, literally, "may not be ruinous to the two of us" (in Latin, ne virtus tua sit damnosa duobus). The strength of a 6-8-11 couple is not the ability to win every fight but the skill of not offering one's chest to each of them: sometimes turning one's back on an argument so as not to turn one's back on each other.

Lisovskaya lists what Strength teaches without any myths, and all of it is visible in this story. From the very start of the relationship, to say what one likes and what one does not — instead of setting the terms of a race. To show feelings openly — in words, not growls. To respect each other so that first place does not have to be won. To share the house fairly and keep work, rest and family in balance.

If quarrels reach the point of threats and home starts to feel frightening, that is no longer a lesson of the tail but a reason to call for help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a lion already tamed
paragraphs: In the Waite–Smith deck, Strength shows a woman closing a lion's jaws. Waite writes that this design differs from the conventional ones in only one point: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers". The lion on Waite's card is already tamed. Ovid's lions are tamed too — "with tamed teeth" — but by Cybele's reins, the Latin frena. The main task of the tail fits into these two pictures: the same lion, and the only question is what holds it — a bridle from outside, or the chain of flowers that Waite describes as a law taken "into the heart of hearts".

On Waite's Lovers, behind the woman stands the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, with the serpent "twining round it". Wen calls it "an apple tree". The golden apples of the myth might have been picked from this tree: the fruit that tempts one off the road.

Waite's Justice sits between pillars with a sword and scales — the woman who, as he says, "is said to be Astræa". Sword and scales in the same hands — this is what Atalanta's race lacked: the rule that cuts and the measure that evens things out held by one judge, not by a goddess tossing weights in from the side.
The cards on the site are drawn differently; everything said here concerns the Waite deck.

sections.h2: The centre and the values of a 6-8-11 couple
paragraphs: For these couples the centre of the matrix — the atmosphere inside the union — is almost always one of two cards: Death (in 59.1%) or The Fool (in 40.6%); The Emperor occurs in 0.3%.

**Death in the centre** is an air of change. Waite writes of Death as "change, transformation and passage from lower to higher". The myth of Atalanta comes from a book whose very title is Metamorphoses, "Transformations". A couple with Death in the centre does not stay the same; the question of the tail is what they turn into: lions in harness, or two people who have grown. In Lisovskaya, the plus here is accepting the partner's past and taking change lightly; the minus is one partner forcing the other to change.

**The Fool in the centre** is an air of freedom. Waite describes The Fool moving "as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him". This is Atalanta before the race, in the woods, where nobody holds the reins. For a 6-8-11 couple such a centre is an antidote to the harness — as long as the freedom rests on trust, and not on each living a life of their own.

"The couple's values" — what the union exists for — split almost evenly in these couples: The World in 34.9%, The Hanged Man in 33.5%, The Empress in 31.7%. The link of each with the myth is our reading.

ul: **The World.** Atalanta's races used to end with her "crowned victorious with festal wreath". Waite's list for The World begins "Assured success, recompense". Wen calls Strength "a foreshadowing of what it will take for a Seeker to reach Judgement and The World". The value of such a couple is a shared wreath, one not won by beating the partner.

**The Hanged Man.** A voluntary halt. Atalanta "delayed her speed" to look at him — and there was more love in that slowing down than in the whole race. Wen notes the progression from reversed Justice — "feeling unjustly wronged when in fact no wrong has been done" — to reversed Hanged Man, "martyrdom". The value here is the pause, not sacrifice on display.

**The Empress.** On Waite's Empress, "the symbol of Venus is on the shield". In the myth Venus is the narrator, the owner of the field where the golden apples grow, and the one nobody thought to thank. The value of such a couple is what the two grow together, not what they win from each other.

sections.h2: How the tail 6-8-11 is built: an example with 05.07.1975 and 14.04.1975
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The person born on 05.07.1975 has the personal tail 12-19-7; the person born on 14.04.1975 has 12-16-4.

The middle 8 came from the two personal middles, The Sun and The Tower, not from the ends of the couple's tail: 6 + 11 would have given 17. This is the second most common combination of personal tails behind 6-8-11 — 28% of these couples. Neither of the two has The Lovers, Justice or Strength in their personal tail. Strength here is one partner's Chariot and the other's Emperor: a will that pushes forward and a power that keeps order.
The rest of this couple's matrix adds more clues:

ul: the couple's centre is 5 + 8 = 13, Death; "The couple's values" is 12, The Hanged Man;

Strength also stands at the point "What to create together": 7 + 4 = 11. Lisovskaya reads this point only in the plus, and Strength in the plus is a couple that charges and strengthens each other. The lion the couple has to tame is the very thing they are to create together;
Justice also stands in the sphere "Attitude to material things": 22 + 22 = 44 → 8. Accounts, plans and reserves here cover not only the relationship but money and things too;
"Image of the couple" is 19, The Sun: from outside a bright, warm couple, the kind no one would suspect of running a race inside.

paragraphs: In all, the tail 6-8-11 is built from 10 combinations of personal tails. The most common are 15-20-5 + 18-6-6 (30% of these couples), 12-16-4 + 12-19-7 (28%) and 15-20-5 + 9-15-6 (15%). In 45.7% of couples, Judgement (20) stands in the personal middle of one of the partners: the couple's justice grows out of somebody's personal judgement.
A couple has no other order of these numbers. A couple's entry is always a multiple of three, so of 6, 8 and 11 only 6 can come first, and 6-11-8 never comes up for any couple.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a race that ends in a tie
paragraphs: In 1972 an American children's album and book, "Free to Be... You and Me", came out. Among its stories is "Atalanta", retold by Betty Miles and read by Marlo Thomas and Alan Alda. A young man called John runs to earn the right to talk with Atalanta. They reach the finish at the same moment. John refuses to marry her unless she herself wants to, they spend the rest of the day talking, become friends and each set off on their own travels — perhaps one day they will marry, and perhaps not.

Our reading: this is an antidote to Ovid, line by line. Instead of growls, the conversation the race was run for. Instead of weights from outside, an equal run. Instead of a prize, a choice each makes alone. The strong version of the tail 6-8-11 is not to stop running, but to run side by side.

The weak version can be seen in stone. In Madrid, on the Plaza de Cibeles, stands a fountain of 1777–1782: the goddess Cybele in a chariot drawn by two lions; the goddess and chariot were carved by Francisco Gutiérrez, the lions by Roberto Michel. Madrid's tourism site says it plainly: "Los leones son Atalanta e Hipómenes" — the lions are Atalanta and Hippomenes. Two marble beasts pull one chariot side by side.
The path of this couple runs between the fountain and the tied race. What helps to walk it:

ul: agreeing on rules openly and revising them when they start to chafe — this is the plus of Justice;
saying thank you after every victory — to each other and to those who helped: not repeating Hippomenes' forgotten incense;
giving way sometimes for no reason and not writing the concession into the minutes;
when the growling rises, stopping: not every fight is worth offering one's chest to;
keeping some strength not only for the chariot of work and status, but for the two of them.

intro: A couple's tail is read in order, and each card has its own role:

ul: **6 · The Lovers — entry to the task.** Where the couple begins and what they want together: attraction, choosing each other, a common language. Resistance hides here too: each wants to be the one chosen, and neither wants to give way.

**8 · Justice — middle of the task.** How the couple travel from the wish to the task: rules, agreements, keeping score, who owes whom. At first this protects against hurt; later it can turn into a race in which both keep minutes.

**11 · Strength — main task.** What the couple have to learn: to handle their own strength, anger and passion so that none of it is aimed at each other. It is read mostly through the minus: rivalry for first place, growling instead of words.

intro: Behind these three roles stands a story told about two thousand years ago — about a girl who could be won only by outrunning her, and a young man who did. It explains this tail better than any definition. But first, the riddle in the numbers themselves.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-8-11 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a tail of the couple's matrix: The Lovers at the entry to the task, Justice in the middle, Strength in the main task. The couple begins with an attraction between equals, lives the union through rules and fair scorekeeping, and learns the main thing — a strength that does not fight the partner: no rivalry for first place, no growling instead of words.

faq.q: Why is there no 6-8-11 in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the task: with 6 and 11 that is 17, The Star, and the personal tail comes out as 6-17-11. In a couple's matrix the middle is the sum of the two partners' middles, so a couple can have 8 there. Neither in one person's tail nor in their money, relationship or talent lines does the triple 6-8-11 occur.

faq.q: How common is the tail 6-8-11 for a couple?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 23 (4.392%) has it: it is the second most frequent of the 97 couple tails. It is built from 10 combinations of the partners' personal tails, and in none of them does either partner have Strength in their personal tail.

faq.q: Can a couple have the tail 6-11-8 or 8-6-11?
faq.a: No. A couple's entry to the task is always a multiple of three, so of these numbers only 6 can come first, and the order 6-11-8 never comes up for any dates. The only couple's tail made of 6, 8 and 11 is 6-8-11.

faq.q: Is the tail 6-8-11 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict and not a forecast. It shows where two people easily slip into rivalry and scorekeeping, and which way to grow: towards a strength that holds itself rather than the other person.

report: A couple with the tail 6-8-11 enters its task as lovers, and risks leaving it as two lions in one harness. This is not a metaphor out of thin air: that is how the myth of Atalanta and Hippomenes ends in Ovid's Metamorphoses, told by Venus herself. The three acts of the myth — the meeting, the race, the transformation — come in the same order as the cards of the tail: The Lovers, Justice, Strength.

Atalanta ran faster than men. An oracle warned her: "while yet living you will lose yourself" — and she set her suitors a condition: whoever outran her would have her as his wife, whoever fell behind would pay with his life. "This must be the condition of a race."

report.h3: The judge who overturned his own verdict

report: Hippomenes comes to the race not as a lover but as a judge: he is ready to condemn the madmen who risk their lives for a wife. Then he sees Atalanta — and passes sentence on himself: "Oh pardon me brave men whom I was blaming, I could not then realize the value of the prize you strove for." Attraction overturns a verdict reached before the meeting. Atalanta's gaze grows "softer, in her vacillating hopes to conquer and be conquered" — and, as Ovid puts it, "she loves and does not know she is in love".

This is what the entry to the task looks like. Two such people often recognise each other in an argument, a competition, at work, where one did not give way to the other: what attracts is someone who is not weaker. The couple's common language is teasing, excitement, "who beats whom", and for a long time it stays fun. The wish is to be together as equals. The resistance lives in that same wish: each wants to be the one chosen, and not to lose while at it.

For Atalanta the condition of the race was a defence against dissolving in another person. The first agreements of such couples often resemble it: "only as equals", "nobody owes anybody anything". That is defence, not love, and the task of the entry is to learn to love oneself inside the couple, not only behind a fence of rules. The roles of the myth are not divided by sex: either partner can be the runner who sets the conditions.

report.h3: A heroine named after the scales

report: Atalanta in Greek comes from ἀτάλαντος, "equal in weight": its root τάλαντον means "scales". She does not need a bridegroom; she needs an equal. The middle of the tail — Justice — lives in the very design of the race. The couple's rules are their own, home-made: splitting the bill, a rota, who does the dishes, "I had the kids on Saturday — Sunday's yours." As long as the scorekeeping helps both, it holds the couple together.

But Venus describes the decisive moment of the race like this: "adding weight to the gold fruit, she held, impeded her with weight and loss of time". **A race meant to be fair was decided by weights dropped onto the scales from outside.** Golden apples are easy to spot in a couple's life: a present instead of an answer, a surprise that cuts the conversation short and wins the argument, a concession made in order to be produced later.

Then comes the unpaid bill. Having won, Hippomenes forgets the goddess — "forgetful of my help, he gave me neither frankincense nor thanks", Venus complains — and she turns against them both. One forgot, and both pay: a couple has one account between two. The scene is familiar: the flat is bought, the wedding is over, the project is delivered — and nobody has said thank you, not to each other, not to those who helped, not to luck. **Gratitude is the payment without which the scales later tip into resentment.** The minus of the middle looks like this: each keeps their own minutes, the fault is always the other's, and the sentence comes out heavier than the offence.

Ovid spends only a few lines on the punishment: "Their faces hold anger; instead of words they give out growls; instead of bridal chambers they haunt the woods; and, feared by others, they champ with tamed teeth the reins of Cybele — lions." Almost every line is a scene from the life of a couple that has not coped with its main task. A quarrel in which both talk and nobody hears. Silent growling: a sigh, a cupboard door banged shut, an answer through gritted teeth. From outside, a strong couple, respected and a little feared. Inside, two people pulling one chariot — a mortgage, a business, the children's timetable — honestly, shoulder to shoulder, without ever looking at each other. The Roman mythographer Hyginus adds that lions are animals to whom the gods deny the union of love. To stay together for ever and stop being lovers.

Neither of the two has Strength in their personal tail: it appears only when the two are added together. So it is in the myth — neither hero was a lion, they became lions as a pair. Waite writes of his Strength card that the lion on it is already subdued and is being led by a chain of flowers. Ovid's lions are tamed too, but by Cybele's bridle. **The main task of this tail lies in what holds the lion: a bridle from outside, or a chain of flowers from within.**

Venus's last advice sounds like a statement of that task: to avoid beasts that never turn their backs but offer their chests in every fight, so that courage "may not be ruinous to the two of us". The strength of this couple is not to win every fight but not to offer one's chest to each of them. To say from the start what one likes and what one does not, instead of setting the terms of a race. To show feelings in words, not growls. To respect each other so that first place does not have to be won. To give way sometimes for no reason and not write the concession into the minutes.

unit.meaning: Your task is strength without rivalry: speak in words, not growls, and run side by side rather than against each other.
